speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Singapore’s reputation as a clean city is a source of national pride.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: High standards of public hygiene have been a cornerstone of our good public health.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Over the years, we have introduced policies and programmes to shape social norms and keep Singapore clean and liveable.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These include anti-littering campaigns, mobilising the community and uplifting the environmental services industry.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Internationally, Singapore is known as a clean and green city.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are overly reliant on efficient cleaning services.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Public toilets in coffee shops and hawker centres are an area of concern and the cleanliness of bin centres and waste disposal areas need to be improved.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Clearly, we still have some way to go to inculcate a strong sense of social responsibility in Singaporeans to do their part to keep public spaces clean.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: At the same time, we remain vulnerable to public health threats.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In 2003, SARS came to Singapore and claimed 33 lives.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have also had to tackle local public health incidents such as the gastroenteritis outbreaks that occurred over 2018 and 2019.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: There are also waterborne health risks from pathogens that lurk in water, such as the Legionella bacteria, which can be transmitted through the inhalation of contaminated airborne water droplets.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Aquatic facilities, such as swimming pools, spa pools and water playgrounds, and aerosol-generating systems, such as cooling towers, can harbour such bacteria.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Between 2000 and 2014, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported around 57 Legionellosis outbreaks associated with aquatic facilities in the US.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: More than 600 fell ill and six people lost their lives.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Similar Legionellosis outbreaks have occurred in Australia, France and the United Kingdom.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: While such outbreaks have not occurred here, we must not be complacent.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For the past eight months, we have been battling the COVID-19 pandemic, a public health crisis unprecedented in scale and impact.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Among the many lessons learnt, an important one is the need for high standards of sanitation and hygiene.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: COVID-19 will not be the last global pandemic that we have to face.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We must shore up our public health defences and be ready to contain emerging outbreaks, when they come.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We can learn from some best practices internationally on managing public health risks more effectively.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: At the 2018 FIFA World Cup in Russia, the Japanese football team and fans earned worldwide praise for practising social responsibility and cleaning up after themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Other than public education, we learnt that a pillar of the national habit of cleanliness in Japan was its Building Sanitation Law.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Large premises, such as schools and shopping centres, are required to conduct thorough cleaning periodically and undertake checks on pest control, indoor air quality and cooling towers.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Japan's legislation also places the responsibility for a building's sanitary conditions on its owners and formalises the role of environmental health personnel to oversee all environmental matters in the premises, including oft-neglected back-of-house areas, such as bin centres.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This has fostered a strong sense of ownership on cleanliness.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It transformed its cleaning industry and processes following the deadly outbreak of MERS in 2015.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Through courses by the International Sanitary Supply Association, cleaners are better-trained and certified on the correct cleaning procedures and disinfection methods.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In New York City, regulations were passed for cooling towers to be registered, tested and regularly maintained after a Legionellosis outbreak in 2015.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This has enhanced New York's capability to manage waterborne public health risks.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These are useful lessons as we seek to strengthen our framework to keep Singapore clean.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have adopted a multi-pronged approach to keep Singapore clean under the national SG Clean movement launched earlier this year.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The SG Clean movement builds on existing hygiene measures and goes further to raise our standards in public hygiene and inculcate a culture of cleanliness, so that we can emerge stronger from COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: First, raising cleanliness standards of premises by working with premises owners; second, transforming the cleaning industry to meet greater demands; and third, inculcating shared responsibility for cleanliness among individuals, as end-users and patrons of premises.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: First, to raise cleanliness standards of premises, we must "Build Right", "Clean Right" and "Audit the Results".

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To "Build Right", we have incorporated in the building plan process, requirements on premises owners, such as the provision of sensor-operated toilet flushing systems and proper layout of bin centres.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Well-designed and well-maintained infrastructure is an enabler of good public health.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: And NEA's SG Clean Quality Mark certifies premises that adopt good cleaning practices.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: A key part of the Bill is to support this thrust under SG Clean, by clarifying lines of accountability for maintaining clean premises and setting clear standards expected of premises owners.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Second, we will continue to transform the cleaning industry to meet increased and more sophisticated demand for cleaning services.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In doing so, we also hope to create more good jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Environmental Services Industry Transformation Map or ESITM launched in 2017 has laid the foundation for this.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For example, by driving technology adoption, upskilling the workforce and enhancing productivity through job redesign and outcome-based contracting.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our cleaners are the unsung frontline heroes of the COVID-19 outbreak, working tirelessly to keep Singapore clean and safe.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will continue to support cleaners as part of the industry transformation journey.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For example, we had introduced the Progressive Wage Model or PWM and PWM Bonus to raise employment standards, facilitate career progression and promote better wages for skilled cleaners.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Since we went into the COVID-19 period, NEA has also collaborated with training institutions to launch new Continuing Education and Training courses on environmental infection control to ensure that cleaners are trained to protect themselves against public health threats at work.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Through this structured training framework, cleaners can become multi-skilled and expect to earn higher wages.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Third, we will promote good personal hygiene and social norms among end-users and patrons at premises.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We launched a campaign under SG Clean earlier this year to promote positive behaviour in our shared spaces and stepped up recently with initiatives on returning trays and using public toilets responsibly in hawker centres and coffee shops.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: More than 5,000 SG Clean Ambassadors have stepped forward to spread SG Clean messages across the country.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: All in, we have a sound framework that has enabled us to maintain good public health.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It will introduce three broad shifts in our approach to environmental sanitation and hygiene.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: First, we will adopt a more proactive approach in guarding against public health threats and institute baseline environmental sanitation standards for routine and periodic cleaning across high-risk premises.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For example, the standards will cover daily cleaning frequencies for high-touch surfaces, such as toilets and lift buttons and oft-neglected areas, such as bin centres; periodic thorough cleaning, say every six months, covering areas that are not easily accessible and not covered by routine cleaning; a pest management plan; and a cleaning and disinfection protocol.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The standards will also specify desired outcome-based cleanliness indicators to be achieved and the tools and training requirements for workers to carry out cleaning effectively.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Third, we will place greater responsibility on the Managers of high-risk premises to ensure that the environmental sanitation standards are met.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: With the support of trained environmental control coordinators and environmental control officers, or ECCs and ECOs in short, the Managers will be required to implement environmental sanitation programmes developed for the premises by the ECCs and ECOs that meet the environmental sanitation standards.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To provide a pipeline of competent ECCs and ECOs, we will introduce a two-tiered competency-based framework.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In general, premises, such as a pre-school or coffee shop, will require an ECC while more complex or multi-tenanted premises will require an ECO, with a higher level of competency to coordinate efforts amongst different tenants within the premises.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Similarly, we will proactively regulate higher risk aquatic facilities and aerosol-generating systems, to manage risks from potential waterborne disease outbreaks.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I will speak first on the environmental sanitation regime.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The new section 62A empowers NEA to designate, with Minister's approval, specified premises for which an environmental sanitation programme is required.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The new section 99A gives powers to the Director-General to issue, approve, amend or revoke codes of practice and standards of performance with respect to the provisions of the EPHA, including programmes and measures relating to environmental sanitation.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: A key feature of this Bill is to clarify the responsibilities for keeping specified premises clean.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Manager of the specified premises must endorse and submit to the Director-General the environmental sanitation programme, implement the programme and any remedial measures recommended by the ECC or ECO.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In accordance with the lines of accountability, the Manager will be responsible for any failure to implement the programme.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To ensure that ECCs and ECOs have the technical competence required to perform their roles, the new section 61A empowers the Director-General to register or refuse to register an individual as an ECC or ECO, and stipulates the circumstances under which the Director-General may suspend or cancel such registration.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The new section 61B provides for appeals to the Minister against the Director-General's decisions made under section 61A.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Notwithstanding upstream preventive efforts under the environmental sanitation regime, we must be prepared to intervene at the first warning signs of a potential health risk.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The new section 62D empowers the Director-General and authorised officers to conduct compliance checks and obtain documents and information for the purposes of the new sections 62A, 62B and 62C.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To effect this, the new section 63 requires the owner or occupier of any premises with a licensable aquatic facility to obtain a licence from the Director-General, prior to its use or operation.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: While we currently have regulations for aerosol-generating systems, such as cooling towers, we do not have a registry of these systems and their locations.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To prevent or manage potential health risks or disease outbreaks, the new section 64 empowers the Director-General to require the cessation of the use or operation of any aquatic facility, or class of aquatic facilities.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This section also empowers the Director-General to require the cessation of the use or operation of a licensable aquatic facility if there has been a contravention of any applicable requirement.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Similar powers are provided under the new section 66B for aerosol-generating systems.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will introduce monitoring powers under the new sections 65 and 66C for the Director-General and authorised officers to conduct compliance checks on any aquatic facility or aerosol-generating system and to obtain documents and information to administer, enforce or ascertain compliance with the requirements in Parts VII and VIIA.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The state of public cleanliness reflects the character of our citizens.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Through collective action and co-ownership, we will forge a cleaner, stronger and kinder Singapore for generations to come.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.25 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.05 pm until 4.25 pm.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is precious quality time, which I wish I have more of.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad to share that I no longer need to change nappies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They are big girls now and use the toilet.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That is of course absolutely good news but also absolutely bad news at times.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Every time they say the words, “Daddy, I need to wee wee”, it sparks a mad crazy frantic race to find a toilet.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Not just any toilet but a male toilet, which has clean seats, which my daughters can sit on.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That, unfortunately, is a hard thing to find, especially in coffee shops and hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The reality is that many of our public toilets stink.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And I am not just talking about the smell.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Often, seats are covered in urine and the entire facility is unhygienic.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is a public health issue that we all need to tackle.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is also not just about toilets but about maintaining cleanliness in premises with high footfall and immuno-vulnerable occupants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The GPC Members will share different perspectives on how we can raise our public hygiene standards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Together, our speeches will articulate four key proposals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We will be raising some of the public’s concerns in our speeches.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, I propose we introduce a grading system for cleanliness at specified premises, starting with public toilets at coffee shops and hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A grading system will help increase hygiene standards in public toilet.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These standards have fallen in recent years, according to an SMU survey aptly named "Waterloo".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Over 25% of the 6,000 respondents said they would not use the toilets in coffee shops and hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our GPC's own public consultation received many comments about bad experiences at such toilets.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One commenter, Mr Tan, said, "Many of our friends have said they rather hold their tummies than to let it out at the kopitiam toilet." But the problem affects us even if we avoid using the toilets.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Mr Jack Sim, Founder and CEO of the World Toilet Organisation said, "Remember that even if you do not use these dirty toilets, the cooks who prepare your food are using them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If there is no soap to wash their hands, you may be eating their dirt." This is a very unpleasant thought but a very real possibility that we need to remember.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It can be similar to the Singapore Food Agency's Food Hygiene Recognition Scheme.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under that scheme, food establishments are rated for their hygiene and must prominently display the grade they receive – A, B, C, or under the new system, Gold, Silver or Bronze.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This provides an objective measure for the general public to determine the level of cleanliness of a food establishment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They can use this information to decide whether to purchase from a food establishment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For a start, will the Ministry consider implementing a similar grading system for public toilets at coffee shops and hawker centres?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A visible, objective benchmark gives operators something to strive towards and could help promote higher standards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second proposal builds on our idea of a grading system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Minister consider linking the grading system to the licensing duration and licensing fees of coffee shops and hawker centres?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, we could offer a slightly longer licence term or lower licensing fees for coffee shops and hawker centres that attain and maintain a certain minimum cleanliness grade.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This provides incentives for premises that have done well, to keep up the good work, and for premises that have not done so well, to raise their standards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In their speeches, other Members of the GPC – Ms Poh Li San, Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Miss Cheryl Chan – will also be sharing their views on a grading system and other incentives for maintaining public toilet cleanliness.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that the Environmental Control Coordinators or ECCs and Environmental Control Officers or ECOs, of specified premises will have to undergo training to be registered with NEA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But I am concerned that their training will not be conducted in suitable languages or formats.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Take, for example, an existing course offered by the Singapore Polytechnic for ECOs in the construction sector.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is conducted entirely in English and requires participants to answer 100 questions in a two-hour electronic examination.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many ECCs and ECOs in the cleaning industry are seniors and would likely struggle with the language requirement and the electronic test-taking component.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister share if such courses for ECCs and ECOs in the cleaning industry will be conducted in more languages and more accessible formats?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It will help operators meet these new requirements without having to replace their existing staff.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let us not allow language barriers and teaching formats to get in the way of cleanliness and safety.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In their speeches, Mr Don Wee and Ms Nadia Samdin will also be speaking on grants to support cleaners in undergoing training courses and career development for our cleaners.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let us remember that higher hygiene standards also means more work for our cleaners.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She said, "Just an hour after I finished cleaning, I come back to find unflushed toilets, water pooling around the basins, and sometimes puddles of urine on the floor." One respondent to our public consultation also raised these fair questions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He asked, "Would not improving cleanliness at these places require more labour?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How do we know that this would not add to the gruelling work that cleaners already have to do?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ultimately, the GPC believes that public hygiene is everyone's personal responsibility and we need to go upstream to solve this problem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While this Bill will help, we urge all Singaporeans to move away from the mindset that cleaners will be there to clean up after us.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should be a "Clean Singapore", not a "Cleaned Singapore".

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Mr Speaker, I rise in support of the Bill.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While COVID-19 has caused widespread economic hardships and taken a toll on many individuals, there are silver linings to this pandemic.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Some silver linings include the rapid digitalisation of the economy and heightened awareness of public and personal hygiene.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: If Singaporeans, as a society are able to capitalise on these silver linings, we will be in a good or perhaps even better position after we ride out this pandemic.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: During the early stages of COVID-19, there were campaigns encouraging the adoption of the 10 Steps Hand Wash, greater conversation on office culture where employees should not fear taking medical leave and not be in the office when unwell.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: These desirable social behaviours and conversations should be encouraged and continued even post-COVID.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As COVID-19 is unlikely to be the last pandemic that the world will see and when the next Disease X may appear, it is a constant worry in the minds of healthcare professionals.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In view of this, it is of paramount importance and perhaps timely to take a more proactive and preventive approach in improving public health and hygiene.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Afterall, these two areas are deemed as the first line of defence against any disease that we may have.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We, as a society should have higher expectations of what being clean and hygienic means.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The achievement of this state should also be a collaboration between public users and the care-takers, instead of having the sole responsibility borne by the latter.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In view of this, I would like to focus on three areas and highlight how we can achieve the aims that are set out.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: First, a greater emphasis on cleanliness in the public domain with the grading system for toilets.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Dirty public toilets are a ubiquitous sight in Singapore and I am sure many of us have experienced this from time to time.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: To address this issue, enforcement of environmental sanitation programmes and having standardised cleanliness metrics are necessary.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The Happy Toilet Programme, which was introduced or started in 2003, is one of such programmes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, it does not seem to have a meaningful impact to-date.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While public toilets are already required to be cleaned at regular intervals, having an industry standard metric of assessment on the desired level of cleanliness could better align everyone and better achieve the aim of improving public health and hygiene.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In the establishment of this industry standard metric of assessment, reference can be derived from the grading of hawker stalls based on the sanitation levels and conditions of management.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Similarly, the grading of public toilets can be used as an objective assessment.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: And second, to elevate importance of social responsibility and communal attitude.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: By placing the entire responsibility on cleaning contractors or Premise Managers to raise the overall standards of public hygiene cannot be the only path forward for us.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It is not only onerous on them but also not fair as the users play a big part of this eco-system.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Thus, a collaborative ownership between the users and caretakers of these public facilities are required.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Let us just look 5,000 km beyond our shores.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We see the shining example of Japan, a place that many would pride them for cleanliness, precision and advanced technology.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: When social responsibility is synonymous to a culture, even smart technologies can be incorporated at public facilities without fear of being damaged.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Think of automatic flushes, bidet gadgets and recently "see-through" public toilets for people to inspect their cleanliness before using them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This indicates an upkeep of these clean public toilets is not just reliant on technologies alone.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The communal mentality is intrinsic and the Japanese way of life appears both in their personal as well as public spaces.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Public spaces are used and treated with respect as the Japanese continually places the interests of the larger good before themselves.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Sometimes I wonder, why are the toilets, such as those in Changi Airport able to keep the high level of sparkling clean conditions whereas toilets in hawker centres and coffee shops leave much to be desired.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: How are we able to maintain our home toilets clean, yet unable to do so in the public?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: If I may posit, it boils down to context and our perception when using these public facilities.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The mentality that this is not my toilet and thus I am not bothered about ensuring the cleanliness and the state I leave it, as there is someone else who cleans after me.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This deplorable mindset must change and has to change now.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We are all users of the public good and only through exercising greater social responsibility can all these public facilities become more desirable.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Perhaps, it is time we take a leaf from Japan, to adopt more communal attitude and let us be proud users of public facilities.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Little actions, such as ensuring that we do not squat on toilet bowls, do not sprinkle water on the floors after washing our hands, proper disposal of papers in the bins go a long way in ensuring the cleanliness of public toilets.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: If we are constantly mindful of what we are doing and treat this the same as our own home toilets, we should be able to do that in the public areas without any fear and without any issue.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: For those caring for young children and seniors, we understand these groups are very vulnerable.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We show our love and our care for them, and always want to ensure they receive the very best.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It is not uncommon to hear of parents lamenting the unsanitary conditions they find in toilets or nursing rooms.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: And I think my colleague, Mr Louis Ng has expressed this quite well.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The impetus to change and care for the public toilets go beyond ourselves.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It is also the message that we wish for our next generation to take away – that we care for our younger ones and our seniors and want to do right for them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Let us not falter and begin today by changing our habits in the use of public resources and treat it like it is our own home.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: And lastly, to rethink the effectiveness of the carrot and stick approach and explore the public health behavioural science to shape societal behaviours and policies.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As we emphasise the need for social responsibility, the question then arises on how do we create this sense of social responsibility to encourage users of public facilities to treat all these facilities with care and sanitation?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: A direct approach would be the traditional use of fines.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Fines has often been used to act as a deterrent for individuals to prevent undesirable societal behaviours, such as littering.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Fines have been used so often that it has been a common joke that Singapore is nothing but a "Fine" city.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While fines can be a quick means to temporary deter an issue, it may not necessarily nip the issue in the bud.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As society evolves, there is stronger call for Singapore to be a gracious and more caring society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Perhaps alternate and gentler ways could be explored in shaping positive societal behaviours.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The concept of incorporating behavioural sciences into policy-making is not a new one in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Several national initiatives had shown evidences of such deep thinking and the fusion of exploring behavioural concepts to enhance the effectiveness of these initiatives.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This paradigm shift in the way of thinking should be lauded.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Under this challenge, the use of incentives was adopted to encourage development of good habits like exercising.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While incentives can be considered as a "carrot" approach, how the challenge was executed revealed signs that it was carefully thought out to ensure that interest in the challenge is sustained and ultimately achieves the objective of encouraging a more active lifestyle.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Have we identified the sweet spot in the use of incentives.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: For example, the amount of incentives and the length of incentives given in the development of these good habits?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: (b) Could we explore similar initiatives such as Nudges to encourage the behavioural change of users in public toilets?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: A well-known example to encourage people to take the stairs instead of the escalators would be the Piano stairs in Stockholm metro where melodious music is played when climbing or going down the stairs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: (c) Besides HPB, the Singapore Police Force has been exploring and getting ideas from the public and the Institutes of Higher Learning on the use of nudges to prevent the public from falling prey on scams.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Could we better understand how effective behavioural sciences have been in policy making?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: COVID-19 is a clear reason why there is no better time than to begin these changes today.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As with all societal changes and benefits, it takes collective effort and thoughtfulness of every individual to effect the change over time.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In the same vein, ensuring the high standards of sanitation requires joint efforts – from the users to the caretakers of the public facilities.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Without which, the actions of a few could thwart the efforts of the broader good.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I am positive that we as a nation would be able to come together and unite in working towards this aspiration of social good.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The aim is to provide enough of a stake that we would see improvements to our living spaces when they fall below acceptable levels.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet while Singapore has an international reputation as a clean city and despite years of Clean and Green campaigns, I believe it is still important to ask ourselves if we are a clean city or a "cleaned" city, as a few of my colleagues have pointed out earlier.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Are we truly a nation where individuals take responsibility to ensure that our environment is clean and hygienic or do we instead see it as someone else's problem?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Do we make messes in our living environments and expect cleaners to do their jobs and clean up after us?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We all agree there is a big distinction in the society which is able to maintain high hygiene standards because people do their parts to keep clean compared with one where low-wage, low-status workers are employed to do their jobs to clean up messes that others have left behind without a second thought.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What does it say about us as a people when we leave our food dishes and rubbish strewn all over the table after a meal and justify it by not wanting the poor cleaners to lose their jobs?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Like many point out, we also have much to learn from the experiences of societies such as Switzerland, Japan and Taiwan which maintain high levels of cleanliness with hardly any litter bins and street sweepers in sight.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Such societies have evolved and have high levels of social consciousness where residents take pride in their surroundings.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This extends to having a culture where people who are sick automatically wear surgical masks to avoid infecting other people without being mandated to do so by law.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Residents also automatically sort their rubbish into different categories to facilitate recycling rather than rely on workers in waste processing centres to do it for them.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While living in Germany, I also remember being extremely conscious about how I would sort out my rubbish for fear of accidentally placing the recyclable materials in the wrong bin and possibly contaminating the material in the entire bin.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: On a weekend trip to Switzerland, stopping for breakfast at a cafe, we witnessed a man at an adjacent table carefully sweeping up the crumbs of the croissant that he just ate before meticulously dusting them onto his plate and returning it to the waiter behind the counter.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The stigma associated with what is traditionally seen as an unskilled, unimportant job can undermine how we view public health and hygiene and lead to under-investment in the industry.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This prevents the implementation of new technologies and digitalisation initiatives that would otherwise raise productivity and make such jobs less physically demanding on our older workers, but also removing some of the stigma associated with being a cleaner.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The wider point here is also one of sustainability, environmental, economic and societal.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We are now facing an uncertain future where the planet is fast running out of time to deal with limited resources and effects of climate change are becoming more real.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We can ill afford to use and consume as if our resources were unlimited.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Even if the cleaning industry looks to more long-term sustainable solutions to provide the services expected of them, we, as in society, must start developing the type of social consciousness required for each one of us to adopt a clean lifestyle.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We could do so by having another look at our Clean and Green campaigns over the years to figure out what has been effective in the past.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Have these campaigns overly emphasised fines, penalties and shaming for specific behaviours with less regard to the reasons behind our actions rather than address wider issues relating to shift in awareness that everyone has a role to play in keeping our shared spaces clean.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A coherent multi-faceted approach that starts from a young age and is tailored to fit our changing society needs to be taken – from punitive measures for those who litter and dirty the environment to public education campaigns at all levels about environmental protection, driving the need to reduce and better manage waste and to foster a pride in our shared spaces.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Youth voices would be extremely important in this and we should fully involve the young from the start in our efforts to effect such changes and driving home the message that our reliance on cheap and elderly labour to clean up after us has to go.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps, it is also time that we look to wisdom espoused by Goethe who wrote: "Let everyone sweep in front of his own door, and the whole world will be clean." This is a shared philosophy that I hope will be one of the legacies that we leave behind for future generations of Singaporeans to come.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We are in the midst of a global crisis, unprecedented in its scale and impact.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Most of us are aware that Singapore is clean because of the hard work of our many cleaners.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, if we all do our part and play a more active role to keep our public environment clean, our collective efforts can help keep costs down.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The high-risk areas listed in the Bill include toilets and other high-touch areas.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many of our public toilets in coffee shops and hawker centres are often very wet.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Sometimes, the wet floors and sink counters are due to leaky taps, shallow sinks and high water pressure or poor user habits.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Wet toilets are both a physical hazard and environmental public health hazard.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This set of specifications will also ensure that toilets that are being upgraded or built will be up to the ES standards.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Useful features include better drainage, better ventilation to minimise foul odours and to speed up evaporation, hand-dryers that are right next to the sinks, and hands-free sensor taps and toilet flushes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With an ageing population, fall prevention should be a priority.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Therefore, the floors of all public toilets should use non-slip materials or coatings.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: All toilets should be upgraded progressively, starting with the older and more poorly designed toilets.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   Many of our public toilets in coffee shops and hawker centres are often wet.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Sometimes, the wet floors and sink counters are due to leaky taps, shallow sinks and high water pressure.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: More often than not, the slippery floors are so because of poor user habits.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Wet toilets are both a physical hazard and environmental public health hazard.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This set of specifications will also ensure that toilets that are being upgraded or built will be up to the ES standards.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Examples of useful features include better drainage, better ventilation to minimise foul odours and speed up evaporation, hand-dryers that are right next to the sinks, and hands-free sensor taps and toilet flushes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With an ageing population, fall prevention should be a priority.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Therefore, the floors of all public toilets should use non-slip materials or coatings.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: All toilets should be upgraded progressively, starting with the older and more poorly designed toilets.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For individuals, public education on the correct toilet etiquette would be useful to keep our toilets clean and dry.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On the subject of sustainability, I am worried about the impact of higher cleaning standards on our environment.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, more gloves and chemicals would be used.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   There is room for improvement in the public hygiene standards of our hawkers centres and coffee shops.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given the large number of customers and thus, the heavy usage of the facilities, such as the tables and toilets, we need a lot more joint effort from all stakeholders to keep these places clean.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These food establishments offer a variety of delicious food at affordable prices for all.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Based on this price level, the operators have budget constraints for the number of cleaners they can employ to keep the food establishments clean.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If everyone makes a conscientious effort to pick up after themselves, return their trays, clean up their tables, refrain from littering, and so on, we will be able to enjoy a clean environment without paying unnecessary additional costs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Another problem eateries have is the presence of pests.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Food remnants attract scavengers such as cockroaches, rats and birds, amongst others.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sometimes when I eat at these places, I see many of these ‘uninvited guests’ flying around and having a ‘party’.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If you are not careful, you could be ‘bombarded’ and may get droppings on you.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sometimes I can see that the food on the tables nearby gets contaminated by these birds.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In recent years, many of these hawker centres and food establishments are forced to install nets to prevent birds from flying in.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Under what circumstances do we need to put in the nets and do the authorities have more plans to extend the installation of nets to more food centres and coffee shops?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Deputy Speaker, Sir, we should also review our pest control regime as pests are vectors for diseases.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the weather gets warmer, pest populations can expand quickly.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have to ensure proper management of food storage and food waste in our food centres.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would there be more incentives, more “carrots” to encourage more people to cooperate?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We may also consider more incentives for owners, stallholders or operators to improve their cleanliness scorecard.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hopefully, this would be a means to an end.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ideally, hygiene and clean habits should become part of our culture, something we all do instinctively, whether or not we would be rewarded for it.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This programme is up to the operators to decide if they want to take it up.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I think the NEA may consider sending strong advisories to obviously poorly designed and maintained toilets to take up this offer and urgently overhaul their toilets in the interest of public health.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Last but not least, may I suggest that we provide incentives for the provision of enclosed areas in our food establishments for smokers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Setting up an enclosed area for them will help to ensure that other customers are protected from second-hand smoke.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, I would like to conclude with my support for the Bill.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: We see our fellow citizens taking ownership of the health of themselves and their families.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: It was inspiring to see how quickly people reacted to the pandemic, abiding by regulations to wear masks, putting sanitisers in lifts and donating masks to those in need.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: This Bill to amend the Environmental Public Health Act arises from the necessity of expanding this to our public spaces.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Singapore has run campaigns to encourage citizens to create a clean and green Singapore.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: However, this changed as our country got wealthier and had access to cheap labour.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Mr Liak Teng Lit, former Chairman of the NEA, reportedly once expressed that Singapore is not a clean City.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Mr Edward de Silva Chairman of the Public Hygiene Council in an article published by today noted that the reliance on cleaners is now entrenched in Singapore's mentality, and thus, it is worthwhile to consider that the overall cleanliness we have in Singapore may not be truly reflective of a collective civic-mindedness on the part of individuals to keep Singapore clean.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: At this juncture, I wish to raise a clarification about the specifics of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: To this end, I would like to seek a clarification on how these assessments will be carried out.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: What are the parameters and principles underlying such assessments?

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: The question of who will take ownership for a good quality of public health comes to mind.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: During the pandemic, we saw how dependent we are on foreign labour as a country to keep Singapore clean.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: What happens if there is another situation that arises, or we do not have access to them.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: We need to ensure that Singaporeans are empowered with a sense of ownership and civic-mindedness towards our country.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: I worry that with more guidelines, and thus potentially, the hiring of more cleaners, we start relinquishing our responsibility in caring for the environment and the people we share our surroundings with.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: We can make comparisons with countries such as Japan and Korea – countries that are known to have a strong sense of civic-mindedness and for being clean, but I think we can draw inspiration from fellow citizens too.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: A resident by the name of Mr Tan, a senior citizen who I met recently on a house visit in Compassvale, shared that he and his neighbours take turns to clean their common corridor on a weekly basis.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: We can also look at people who organise beach clean-ups at places like East Coast Park and Changi Beach, or those who organise ground-up initiatives to help those who are unable to spring-clean their homes.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: We even count the World Toilet Man himself, Jack Sim, as a fellow citizen who has been a crusader of upholding good personal hygiene.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: To encourage citizens to take ownership of their surrounds, we need to encourage civic-mindedness in youths by exposing them to more community-based programmes and weaving the themes of community building into our schools.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: We need to make students responsible for the cleanliness of their schools and we need to encourage people to recycle.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: The state should seek to improve recycling facilities in residential areas.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: We can build on the reputation of a clean and green city.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   I support the Environmental Public Health (Amendment) Bill introduced by the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The ongoing global pandemic has given us a strong impetus to review our public hygiene regulation and enforcement framework.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We should not miss this opportunity to raise the public hygiene standard.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We should learn the lessons and the health reform opportunities presented by the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If we do not gain the experience nor reflect upon ourselves, we would waste this learning opportunity to enhance our ability to resist future health crises.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Such premises include nursing homes, kindergartens, public toilets and rubbish collection centres.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The new requirements will help our fight against COVID-19 and mitigate future public health risks.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One of the most common complaints about public hygiene is about the toilets in our hawker centres and coffee shops.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, owners and operators have often told me that they are worried about the higher costs of cleaning.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They may not be able to absorb the higher cost and may need to pass part of it to their customers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They are concerned that they may lose some business as a result.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also have some concerns with the requirement for premises managers to be identified and held accountable for adhering to the ES standards.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope that for the implementation of this new measure, building and premises owners will be required to provide proof that they give premises managers the authority and requisite resources to carry out their duties.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I seek the assurance of the Ministry that designated employees will not be held responsible in the event that environmental sanitation standards are not met due to insufficient resources.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Take the two coffee shops at Brickland’s blocks 803 and 810 for example.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The coffee shop aunties and assistants are my residents.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They are managing 2 roles at the same time, making coffee, serving tea and cleaning as well.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They are the frontline workers providing essential services, but their salaries are not very high.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am very concerned about their working conditions after the new regulations come into force.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English):	Customers, who desire cleaner toilets, also worry about the prices of their favourite hawker meals going up.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We would also want to ensure that hawker and coffee shop meals remain accessible and affordable for the less privileged Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The higher demand for cleaning due to the pandemic has already led to a labour shortage.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is a sector which attract fewer Singaporeans and on top of this difficulty, there is a limit on the number of foreign workers we can hire.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Perhaps, for some premises, it may be viable to deploy robot cleaners, for example.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, it would be challenging to use robot cleaners in the toilets of our hawker centres and coffee shops, due to the terrain and space constraints.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the face of this manpower crunch, how are we going to meet the new environmental sanitation (ES) standards?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Do we have plans to draw more Singaporeans or PRs into this sector or will we need to re-adjust manpower policies?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will higher wages alone be sufficient to attract and retain local workers?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will the Ministry persuade the Singapore public to pay more for local workers, while at the same time, ensure that the less privileged ones amongst us do not have to bear the burden of the higher cleaning costs?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the face of limited manpower, we must help our cleaners to become more efficient and productive.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I seek the Ministry's assurance that it will become a permanent training programme, with refresher and upgrading courses in the future.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will ensure that our cleaners will meet ES standards and be equipped to deal with potential new health hazards.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am also very glad to note the new Toilet Improvement Programme launched by NEA last Friday.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I strongly urge them to tap on this programme to fund the necessary renovations and measures.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: New toilets can be redesigned to make it easier to be kept clean.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, round sloped sinks are better than flattish square or rectangular sinks which tend to accumulate debris in corners.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Taps, soap dispensers, toilet flushes and doors can be operable through sensors or with foot pedals.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In order for us to benefit from a higher sanitation standard, we must all take joint responsibility for our environment and do our part to keep our surroundings clean.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There is thus an important role for public education.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am interested to hear more about the Ministry's efforts in this area.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, Singaporeans' civil-mindedness has a lot of room for improvement.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If each of us do our part and encourage those around us to do their parts, our collective effort will go a long way to keep Singapore cleaner, reduce the need for cleaning and minimise the cleaning costs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The introduction of the amendments is timely considering that the COVID-19 pandemic has magnified the importance of individual and public hygiene.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is an excellent opportunity to improve the nation's public health infrastructure beyond COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A strong healthcare system needs an equally robust hygiene framework to keep up the fight against the current pandemics and future ones.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The amendments, which include the implementation of mandatory standards and greater accountability on stakeholders, complement the SG Clean Movement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The new rules will also play an integral role in increasing the effectiveness of safe management measures as we work towards a gradual and safe reopening of our economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I will now detail two points for the consideration of the Minister and one query to allow for the better integration of the amendments for relevant stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, the benefits arising from the mandatory appointment of ECCs and ECOs in premises are two-fold: not only will it complement our efforts to improve public hygiene infrastructure, but it also fits well within our national push to expand upskilling and employment opportunities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In supporting these enhanced rules, I recognise that the Labour Movement has a pivotal role to play in ensuring that companies have sufficient trained workers to comply with the rules with greater ease.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Currently, institutions such as NEA and Singapore Polytechnic offer ECO training courses, but these might be tailored to old requirements for maintaining good environmental practices within construction sites.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our NTUC social enterprises can increase training capacity for ECCs and ECOs in line with the amended Section 62B.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Additionally, we could potentially look into dove-tailing of ECC and ECO work with Safe Management Officer responsibilities to better coordinate businesses' efforts for safe re-opening.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Second, as we work towards baseline cleaning standards and increased public hygiene responsibilities, we must remember to keep broader goals in mind.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must progressively aim to shift from Government-led initiatives towards a structure where all stakeholders take ownership.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: To this end, I put forth two recommendations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, the new environmental sanitation programmes cannot work without well-trained workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They must also be paid fairly so that we can attract more workers to join the industry.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Businesses must adopt outcome-based procurement practices and Government give recognition to companies that work towards increased productivity with the adoption of technology.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Second, we must recognise that Singapore relies heavily on cleaning services to ensure the cleanliness of public areas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Despite Governmental and businesses' efforts in working towards a cleaner Singapore, we must remember that this responsibility lies in the individual too.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Take the example of returning of trays in Food & Beverage establishments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Public education is thus, vital, in working towards a cleaner Singapore and this initiative will instil greater individual responsibility to keep Singapore clean.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Lastly, I have one query relating to the fines imposed in contravention of the amended sections.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The contravention of the relevant sections in the amendments in section 62A(5), 62B(3), 62C(6), 63(2), 66A(7) by the Manager of any specific premises/owner/occupier would constitute an offence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This serves as an effective deterrent to the management of smaller premises, all those without as much resources.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, I am concerned that the deterrent effect of the fine may not be as effective for well-resourced entities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Notwithstanding the suggestion, I stand in support with the amendments which will play an important role in chartering the nation's journey to successfully sail through the COVID-19 pandemic and beyond.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have had to build up our resilience as a society, while we stay home to flatten the curve.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But not everyone could do this. "Stay home because we can't" – this was one of the viral phrases first expressed by essential workers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: During this time, many essential workers were required to step-up the cleaning regimes, their efforts on this front kept us safe.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As Singapore plans for Phase Three, gradually reopens and allows for more public movement, we must as a society remain vigilant.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The events of the past few months have made a few things clear.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Government and pandemic response teams need to be constantly receptive to new information and err on the side of caution and we must all play our part.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The pandemic has highlighted the importance of civic mindedness and the responsibility shared between Government, businesses and the public to keep each other safe.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am supportive of this Bill and have four points to make on the amendments.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, the pandemic has highlighted the important role essential workers play in keeping Singapore safe.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The establishment of the environmental control coordinator and environmental control officer roles can be a step towards elevating the essential worker and creating pathways for career development in environmental health as individuals become experts in the subject matter.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They offer an opportunity for training, skill acquisition and capability development.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I sincerely hope that businesses will look inwards for talent that can be nurtured when thinking about these appointments, so as to enable our cleaners to develop new skills and earn more.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also hope that the Ministry can provide employers with support on the above and discourage organisations from simply outsourcing these functions.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am unsure whether these roles, if fulfilled by part-time external workers, will have an actual effect on improving cleanliness standards.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One suggestion would be for the Ministry to consider a reduction in training fees for businesses that send existing Singaporean employees to be upgraded and certified.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, one of the biggest lessons we have learned from COVID-19 is the importance of prompt and timely action in our response to pandemics.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have seen instances in the early days of COVID-19, where conservancy workers and cleaners were merely equipped by their employers with masks, disinfectants and simple cloths.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In short, I would like to suggest the Ministry to take collaborative approach when working with premise managers and workers to meet the new standards set out in this Bill, especially in the early days of transition and to prioritise safety of our essential workers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Third, I understand that the amendments also envision Codes of Practices which will set out sector-specific standards required as part of the ES regime.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It would be helpful if the Ministry can explain why there are different sector-specific standards and whether ECC and ECO skills and training will be transferable across the industries.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Like we did with SARS in 2003, we have and we are still learning from COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While reactive learning is, unfortunately, going to be necessary when dealing with a pandemic, we can take a proactive approach by working with the public to transform Singapore from a cleaned city, to a clean city.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must find more effective ways of working with the public to imbue a culture of personal responsibility in the cleanliness of the facilities that we share, as they do in countries, such as Japan, which has a national habit of Marie Kondo-ing and keeping things clean and tidy.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that we must double down our efforts in building a responsible culture to keep our public toilets clean, return our trays and utensils so that food scraps do not attract unwanted pests which carry diseases, and picking up after ourselves in shared spaces.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, a few words in Malay.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Malay):   Frontline workers especially cleaners play a very important role in keeping the environment clean.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, these policies will not be enough in our efforts to combat the spread of the COVID-19 outbreak if Singaporeans do not play their part to maintain our environmental hygiene.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must cultivate good habits and promote a culture where cleanliness is prioritised no matter where we are, whether inside or outside our homes.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, ultimately, our laws reflect social norms and will only be effective when implemented well.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This will help reduce the risks posed by diseases and create a safer environment for all to live, work and play.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In support of this Bill, I would like to also highlight that more of us are working from home as a result of this pandemic, which have implications on the current way we regulate environmental public health.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Given this recent trend, there are now more smokers as well as non-smokers who are working from home.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Many industry experts expect this new norm of working from home to continue well after this pandemic ends.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This is due to the benefits of remote working for individuals as well as for corporates.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As circuit breaker measures kicked in on 7 April, it is likely that the number of complaints to NEA could have been higher since the last report.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The dangers of second-hand smoke as a silent killer, the smell and residue from nicotine and the irritation to the nose and throat are well documented and have been discussed previously in this House, so I will not belabour this point.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Of the resident feedback that I have received about neighbours smoking, at least half of those were smoking near open windows or doors.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Today, the solution to limit the effects of second-hand smoke floating from a neighbour is for the non-smokers to shut their windows or doors.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: A practical way is to perhaps require resident smokers to close their windows and doors when they smoke and, of course, to go down to the open spaces at the ground floor if they have kids around.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This solution aligns to existing NEA regulations which require windows of private vehicles to be fully wound up so that the second-hand tobacco smoke is expelled when the driver smokes in certain areas.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: A similar parallel could be drawn to the smoking rooms at hotels where doors and windows are closed so that the impact to other hotel occupants are minimised.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In this way, a requirement like this will protect the rights of all parties concerned – for residents to smoke at home as well as non-smokers and neighbours to protect their health.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, this proposal provides the non-smoker the added option of closing their windows or doors.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that while such a policy does not completely eliminate the impact of second-hand smoke, it can however significantly reduce the impact of smoke experienced by residents living next to a smoker neighbour.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Importantly, this proposal is a balanced approach that draws a line and recognises the need for both sides and not just the party whose health is being endangered to play their part.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It will also go a long way towards reducing the tension between neighbours as our living spaces become more compact.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This will be yet another step taken in the right direction that does not add to the complexity of existing enforcement measures.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I hope Minister Grace Fu will study this and consider amending the regulations in future to address this environmental health issue that is at the heart of many HDB and condominium residents.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   The COVID-19 pandemic has made us to be more concerned about our health.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I support the timely amendment to the Bill to raise the hygiene standards of pre-schools, eldercare centres as well as swimming pools, water playground and the central air-conditioning systems, as well as to state clearly the responsibilities of premises managers.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This is to better protect the health of our people and giving them peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, as a result of the pandemic, more people are working from home, including many smokers.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Recently, many residents complained that second-hand smoke from their neighbours have forced them to close their doors and windows, which they felt was unfair.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Government will pay more attention to the health hazards of passive smoking.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I think a feasible way is to require smokers to close their doors and windows when they smoke at home, so that their right to smoke will not be affected, and the health of their neighbours will be protected.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
