text: At the same time, this recommendation is in line with the NEA requirement for in-car smoking.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Hotels have a similar practice for in-room smoking.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that NEA will study the feasibility on the suggestion in depth.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: (In English): In conclusion, the new policies in this amendment will give residents greater peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In the longer term, this will be a significant boost to the environmental public health of all in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Singapore must quickly fulfil the critical requirements to enable us to safely reopen our hub to the region and the world.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It requires proper planning and implementation regimes to safeguard us from the spread of COVID and future pandemics.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must also inculcate basic public health sanitation habits as part of our culture and DNA.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It has to become our way of life.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is not solely the responsibility of the business owner or the manager of the premises.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This is our shared responsibility to safeguard one another.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: For this amendment, I would like to highlight that we will should also consider the impact and opportunities for SMEs and the environmental sanitation industry.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: SMEs may find it challenging due to their limited resources and limited manpower.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In this climate, SMEs are doing their best to sustain their core businesses and protect the livelihood of workers.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: However, SMEs also understand the importance of these measures.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In the near term, we must ensure that there are sufficient resources for ECCs and ECOs to get trained, certified and avoid down time.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: There must also be sufficient sanitation service providers to ensure that it is priced competitively to help manage the operating cost of SMEs.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):   SMEs have limited financial and human resources, which is a challenge for them.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In this difficult economic environment, SMEs are doing their best to sustain their businesses and protect workers' livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: However, SMEs also recognise the importance of these measures.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We should help our SMEs meet this new requirement.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: A phased approach is needed to help SMEs implement these regulatory requirements to meet the required standards.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In the near term, we must ensure that there are sufficient resources to train and certify ECO and ECCs to avoid work stoppage.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: There must also be sufficient sanitation service providers to ensure that prices are reasonable and help SMEs manage costs.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, in English, please.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: With the limited manpower in Singapore, we must also be cognisant of how we help Singaporeans develop their full potential as they take on new roles.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: These skills must be multi-disciplinary, transferrable and relevant to a broad set of job opportunities.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This is opportune to the industry to chart expertise development, career progression roadmaps and transferrable skills laterally and vertically within the sanitation and public health eco-system.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The training and upskilling of new coordinators and officers should be steeped in the understanding of business, law, science and technology.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It should be a journey of building expertise and in the spirit of strengthening Singapore's resilience and relevance.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We need to make sure that no one gets left behind.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must design progressive steps for everyone to feel confident to have the capacity to build expertise and skills as a way of life.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must remember that though it is important to safeguard and enforce higher standards of public health and sanitation, we must not forget that every step must be to build a stronger, more confident and competitive Singaporean workforce that is agile and competent.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I am in agreement with Minister for Sustainability and Environment, Ms Grace Fu, that "we need to strengthen Singapore's environmental public health resilience, to safeguard Singaporeans against the current pandemic and dengue outbreak, as well as future public health threats".

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We must not further delay the important step in raising cleaning standards.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: These invisible bacteria and viruses in the toilets are quite hardy unless they are being neutralised by disinfectants regularly.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Frequent habits, such as using mobile phones while in the toilets, further exacerbate the transmission of diseases beyond the washroom.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Hence, if the dirtiest places can be kept clean and generally germ-free, infectious disease transmission can be well-controlled at source.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is common knowledge that when it is everybody's problem, then fewer people will act on it.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Many public washrooms, especially in hawker centres and coffee shops, are not well kept.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Unfortunately, there are many irresponsible culprits who reflect poor civic responsibility and leave the responsibility of cleaning up to the many senior uncles and aunties who have to clean for a living.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is only common sense that, even with the EPHA, it would be an uphill battle if users are irresponsible.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Two weeks ago, during my house visit, I spoke with a resident who has worked for many years as a cleaner for Sembawang Town Council.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This resident shared with me that it is very frustrating for him to keep cleaning the mess left all over the place.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Items, such as empty beer cans and cigarette boxes, are often thrown on the basketball courts.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Good practices start at home and in schools.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I recall when I was in Primary school, my school mates and I have toilet cleaning duties during our school camps.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It was a little humbling at first but, after a while, we learnt to master the techniques of using different brushes and detergents for different locations.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Till now, I continue using these skills I learnt in school and I will always keep my toilets at home sparkling clean.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It may be a good idea to start training our younger ones from a tender age, so that they maintain these good habits into adulthood.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Let us all do our part and be more civic-minded when using the public toilets and consider the 59,000 cleaners who are already past 60 years old.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Let us also consider who will be replacing these uncles and aunties once they stop working.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Next, I would like to touch on the amendments to strengthen environmental sanitation controls in premises.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Gyms, studios, sports halls and so on of all sizes and for various sports, during pre-COVID days, are often densely packed during the peak hours, with energetic sports enthusiasts who are frequently soaked in profuse perspiration after a good workout.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: According to a 2014 study by the School of Public Health at University of Memphis, gym equipment can be dirtier than a toilet seat.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Many of these sports venues, especially the gyms and studios, are enclosed within an air-conditioned environment, with no natural ventilation.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The washrooms and shower facilities are also often packed, especially during the morning and evening peak periods.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: There are inconsistencies in the housekeeping hygiene standards as some gyms and studios ensure thorough cleaning and some do not.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: On this note, would it be effective or fair to foist the responsibility and accountability solely on premises managers?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Under the environmental sanitation regime, the Bill will require premises managers to assume the responsibility to meet the mandatory environmental sanitation standards and take greater ownership to proactively clean their premises through the implementation of a systematic and preventative cleaning routine.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In childcare, schools, nursing homes and even sports venues, the users do pay sufficient regular fees and these fees will allow the business owners to provide a reasonable standard of hygiene and cleanliness.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, we need to look into the hawker centres and coffee shops.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We need to ensure that these premises meet the environmental sanitation standards.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Most public toilets no longer collect a fee to use the toilets and the amendments to EPHA must not result in a regressive step where patrons are then required to pay a fee for the use of the washrooms.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: So, we need to look into the inevitable additional manpower and higher costs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: These cost increases may be passed on to the tenants and, in turn, to the patrons in the form of higher food prices.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: To nurture a proactive "keep-clean culture", I would also suggest MSE consider a carrot-and-stick approach rather than just a stick approach.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We could incentivise premises owners to consistently maintain a high standard of cleanliness and hygiene, by providing a clean property tax rebate.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Dedicated efforts and focus must be taken to consistently score well on every inspection.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I think incentives will go a long way to motivate both the premises owners and the cleaning crew to do more than just the bare minimum.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Another suggestion is to promote active citizenry in reporting venues with poor sanitation standards directly via an app to NEA.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The public can be the eyes and ears on the ground to help NEA inspectors focus on premises that require their attention.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The premises owners must be taken to task.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In addition, perhaps NEA could consider an annual contest for the public to vote in the top three venues with the cleanest toilets into the Hall of Fame, as well as the worst three venues with the dirtiest toilets into the Hall of Shame.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: No one wants to belong to the latter, so such a contest may put some social pressure to keep premises owners motivated and this could possibly be more effective than summons and fines by NEA.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Now, I would like to conclude the key points raised by the Government Parliamentary Committee in Mandarin.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, I shall now conclude the key points and suggestions raised by the MCE GPC in Mandarin.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Premise owners can also consider implementing operation processes or additional equipment that will raise efficiency of cleaning.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: For example, coffee shop owners can consider implementing a more effective pest control solution or automated vacuum and washing equipment.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In addition, F&B owners can also attract more patrons by maintaining a higher hygiene standard.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In schools, teachers should teach the students the good habits of maintaining hygiene and cleanliness.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: At home, parents should also encourage their children to partake in the household chores.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In public, citizens should also maintain the cleanliness of surroundings, to reduce the reliance on our cleaners.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The reason is that other than COVID-19, there could be other more deadly transmission diseases in future.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Therefore, we should start now and prepare ourselves well, to prevent such horrible viruses from endangering precious lives.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Otherwise, the cleaners may not understand the course contents and find themselves failing the course and in turn losing their jobs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In addition, we also encourage Singaporeans from all walks of life, to express their gratitude towards the cleaners for many years of hard work and their contribution in keeping Singapore clean.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Their thoughtful comments and suggestions reflect the importance that we collectively place on preserving a clean and healthy environment for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Members have raised pertinent points which can be broadly summarised as follows.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: First, while the environmental sanitation regime focuses on Premises Managers taking responsibility for the cleanliness of their premises, we must also instill greater social responsibility for public hygiene, especially on the part of end-users.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Second, even as we lean on Premises Managers to take concrete steps to improve cleanliness, we must help them manage compliance costs.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Third, we must build on the capabilities of all key partners within the cleaning eco-system, including the cleaning industry, cleaners, Environmental Control Coordinators (ECCs) and Environmental Control Officers (ECOs).

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Miss Cheryl Chan, Mr Don Wee, Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Ms Nadia Samdin, Ms Poh Li San, Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Derrick Goh, Ms Joan Pereira, Ms He Ting Ru and Ms Raeesah Khan have spoken passionately about the need for shared responsibility for public cleanliness, especially on the part of consumers and end-users.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Members called for a shift away from the mindset of not caring about public spaces or amenities, simply because it is not our own.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Building shared responsibility is a key thrust of our SG Clean movement.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We are working with partner organisations and SG Clean Ambassadors to communicate simple yet important social norms on cleanliness, such as binning used tissues and litter, and returning one’s tray at hawker centres.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We have also been exploring the use of behavioural science approaches to shape habits, as suggested by Miss Cheryl Chan and Ms Poh Li San.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: NEA has piloted the use of visual and audio cues to nudge users to return their trays at hawker centres.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: NEA has also piloted behavioural nudges such as placing posters with normative and emotive messages, in strategic locations, to encourage users to keep public toilets clean and dry.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will continue to push on this front.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We fully appreciate the concerns of businesses, especially in this difficult economic climate that we are in right now.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Premises Managers should view the enhanced measures as the best insurance against potentially much larger costs should an outbreak happen due to unsanitary conditions.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Businesses benefit from having good environmental sanitation that protects the health of their customers, employees and, as one Member has mentioned, the chefs that are working at the premises.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Conversely, lapses in public health can cost them dearly.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The F&B outlets and childcare centres involved in the gastroenteritis outbreaks in 2018 and 2019 know this from first-hand experience.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Against the backdrop of COVID-19, businesses are prioritising cleanliness and hygiene as assurance to customers and to woo them back.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, cleanliness at this time fully reflects the importance of environmental sanitation and public hygiene.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: From the outset, we have adopted a pragmatic approach to ensure adequate standards, while managing the impact on businesses.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We have been working closely with sectoral leads, such as MOE, MSF, Early Childhood Development Agency and Singapore Food Agency or SFA to develop environmental sanitation standards that take into account the needs and constraints of each sector.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As an illustration, let me share how we are working with SFA and coffee shop owners to implement an environmental sanitation regime, while managing business costs for coffee shop owners.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: NEA is working closely with coffee shop owners to put in place a regime that is practical and effective.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The coffee shop owner who is the Premises Manager may appoint his outlet supervisor as the ECC.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Some Members have voiced concerns about many of our elderly cleaners not being able to meet the needs or the standards required of an ECC.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The outlet supervisor, after the requisite training, will have the competencies to tailor an appropriate environmental sanitation programme and I would say here it is tailoring because we will come up with a standard template that the different sectors can tailor to their own circumstances.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Alternatively, the owner may double-up as the ECC.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The environmental sanitation programme will focus on key areas that impact public health.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: For example, it will lay out daily cleaning frequencies for high-touch surfaces, such as seats and table-tops, as well as public amenities such as toilets.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: There must also be thorough periodic cleaning of hard-to-reach areas such as ceiling beams and overhead fixtures which can harbour rats and birds.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The coffee shop owner will be required to conduct a comprehensive pest management survey periodically, say once every six months.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Such inspections can surface defects for rectification, such as crevices to be sealed.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The ECC will be trained in the basics of pest management so he can monitor pest management works.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: These preventive measures, coupled with good housekeeping, go a long way in tackling the root causes of the pest issues highlighted by Mr Gan Thiam Poh.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In the first half of next year, NEA will refine the environmental sanitation standards in consultation with industry stakeholders, issue the Code of Practice, and train the ECCs.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The training syllabus, which focuses on the basics of hygiene, is applicable to all sectors.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will start with a six-month advisory period for sectors to gradually adapt to the regulatory requirements, before enforcement begins.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, that would take us to the end of the year and we will start enforcing in 2022.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Ms Poh Li San and Ms Nadia Samdin have asked to roll out the environmental sanitation regime to other premises and Ms Raeesah Khan has also asked about the framework in deciding which sectors to go first.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, we will start with implementation at higher risk premises with immuno-vulnerable occupants such as eldercare and childcare facilities; premises with high footfall such as coffee shops and hawker centres; or premises with a history of outbreaks.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will consider their suggestions when extending the regime to other premises in subsequent phases.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This is also in response to Mr Shawn Huang's suggestion that we should phase out the implementation so that there is time for capacity to be built into the industry.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Don Wee, Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Ms Poh Li San, Ms Joan Pereira and Mr Shawn Huang raised concerns about the cost impact of enhanced cleaning requirements.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will help businesses, especially the small players, manage costs.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will allow flexibility for Premises Managers of small businesses to double up as ECCs.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: An ECC will be allowed to supervise cleaning works at a few branches or outlets as long as he is able to handle the workload.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will also help Premises Managers improve infrastructure and capabilities to enhance cleanliness, such as through NEA’s Toilet Improvement Programme for coffee shops and hawker centres which Ms Joan Pereira might be interested in.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We are also exploring with SkillsFuture Singapore or SSG on the possibility of subsidising training costs for ECCs and ECOs, a suggestion raised by Ms Nadia Samdin.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The third cluster of issues, which was raised by Mr Don Wee, Ms Nadia Samdin, Mr Louis Ng and Mr Desmond Choo, is about future-proofing the cleaning industry by raising capabilities and supporting the workers.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As Mr Don Wee pointed out, the COVID-19 pandemic has exacerbated manpower shortages in the cleaning industry.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Indeed, the industry is a growth area in jobs.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And we want existing jobs to expand in skills and productivity so that more Singaporeans can get better paying jobs in the cleaning industry.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This gives a strong impetus to accelerate the pace of digitalisation and automation in the cleaning industry to enhance productivity.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This is a key thrust under the Environmental Services Industry Transformation Map.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Cleaning companies have tapped on the enhanced Productivity Solutions Grant to adopt technology to overcome manpower constraints.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Lionsbot, a local start-up which sells and rents out cleaning robots, has seen an increase in demand for their robots, with 80% more inquiries since the pandemic started.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: LionsBot will be building 300 autonomous cleaning robots and progessively deploying them across Singapore to scrub, mop, vacuum, sweep, shine and even transport cleaning equipment.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The cleaning robots can be rented by cleaning companies on a subscription basis so they do not need to invest in ownership and maintenance.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We are also upskilling workers in the cleaning industry.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Workforce Singapore, in partnership with NEA and the Environmental Management Association of Singapore, has rolled out a new Place-and-Train Programme for Cleaning Specialists for Disinfection Services in August 2020.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This programme enables cleaners and jobseekers to reskill to take on the role of a cleaning specialist.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: With enhanced skillsets, these individuals can take on more specialised and skilled job roles that offer better salaries and career prospects.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As Members rightly pointed out, we must ensure that workers are fairly rewarded and can make a decent living.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: All cleaning businesses are required to provide wages stipulated under the Progressive Wage Model or PWM.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Other measures are in place to ensure fair labour practices in the cleaning sector.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: MOM worked with tripartite partners to encourage premises to provide rest areas for outsourced workers like cleaners.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In view of the COVID-19 situation, NEA and MOM worked with tripartite partners to advise service buyers and providers to ensure the safety and health of cleaners, manage their workload, and remunerate them appropriately for additional responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The effectiveness of the environmental sanitation regime does not just depend on the cleaning industry; it also requires that ECCs and ECOs have the knowhow to assist the Premises Manager.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Louis Ng and Mr Desmond Choo have spoken on this.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Training for ECCs and ECOs will be customised to their needs and literacy levels as far as possible.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: For example, to cater for adult learners, the course does not stipulate educational qualifications and can accept trainees so long as ECCs can attain Workplace Literacy and Numeracy or WPLN Level 5 for reading, listening, speaking and writing.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: ECOs will require WPLN Level 7, or Level 6 with two years of relevant working experience.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This basic proficiency is necessary, as the ECCs and ECOs need to learn how to develop an environmental sanitation programme and convey clear instructions to cleaners.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if the training course for ECCs and ECOs can be conducted in more languages and are suitable for seniors.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Initially, training will be conducted in English but NEA will review the need to offer the course in more languages, depending on the trainees’ needs.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Taking into account employers’ needs, NEA will work with training providers to make the training course as concise as possible without compromising quality, and will provide bite-sized information or pictorial guides where possible.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As we gradually extend the environmental sanitation regime to more premises, there will be greater demand for competent ECCs and ECOs.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Several Members, including Ms Poh Li San and Miss Cheryl Chan spoke about public toilets, and the importance of practising social responsibility in keeping them clean.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Louis Ng and Miss Cheryl Chan suggested introducing a cleanliness grading system for public toilets and tying it to licensing duration or fees for hawker centres and coffee shops.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This overall approach of education and enforcement is broadly in line with our multi-pronged strategy to improve public toilet cleanliness.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Our first strategy is to improve design and infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As part of this, NEA is reviewing requirements for proper toilet design in the Code of Practice on Environmental Health, setting up model toilets in hawker centres and supporting infrastructure upgrade under the Toilet Improvement Programme.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Second, NEA will step up surveillance and enforcement.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Through the environmental sanitation regime, we will foster effective cleaning of toilets by mandating baseline standards.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This is complemented by training programmes for toilet cleaners.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We have also tightened penalties against toilet lapses since 1 April 2020 and NEA will continue with surveillance efforts through regular inspections.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Third, NEA will ramp up public education and promote good toilet etiquette.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: You may have heard of our recent Public Toilet Cleanliness Initiative, where NEA partnered the Restroom Association of Singapore to promote good toilet habits.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In line with Ms Poh Li San’s suggestion on involving citizens’ contribution, and Miss Cheryl Chan made a smiliar suggestion, we have installed feedback panels in some hawker centre toilets, to gain insights on users’ perceptions and make more targeted infrastructural improvements and cleaning efforts.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, do look out for the “Loo of the Future” Challenge to crowdsource for innovative toilet design ideas in the coming months.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: On Mr Louis Ng and Miss Cheryl Chan’s suggestion of a cleanliness grading system, our primary focus for now is to support the premises in achieving a set of baseline environmental sanitation standards.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This will motivate coffee shops to maintain good track records and uphold cleanliness in their premises.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Notwithstanding the focus of the Bill, Members have also spoken passionately and more broadly on a host of other environmental public health related matters, such as pest control, bird nuisance, tray return, smoking and littering.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: For better focus on the Bill, I will not address them one by one, specifically.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: These interrelated issues show that public health is multi-faceted and the solutions must also be multi-factorial.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This is why all users must play their part if we are to truly move the needle on public hygiene.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: While the Manager can keep his place clean and safe, individuals must take responsibility to maintain good personal hygiene.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This is not just about safeguarding public health, but also building a more gracious society.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In properly disposing of our used tissues for example, we help protect our cleaners, many of whom are elderly, from biohazards in their work environment so that they can work safely.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I ask everyone to work with us to make Singapore a truly clean and liveable home, and instil a national culture of cleanliness.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Good public hygiene will help us get over the current pandemic and be better prepared for the next outbreak.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We must do our utmost to keep Singapore safer and stronger.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: (In Mandarin):   Public hygiene must remain our first line of defence against disease outbreaks.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The SARS outbreak in 2003 claimed 33 lives.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The COVID-19 pandemic we are facing will not be the last global pandemic that we have to face.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Hence, we must sustain our efforts in ensuring a clean environment and maintaining good personal hygiene.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This will safeguard public health, and protect lives.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: NEA will work with sector leads and industry partners in the coming months to co-develop these environmental sanitation standards applicable to their respective sectors and ensure that the standards are customised and fit for purpose.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We are mindful of the operating and compliance costs to premises managers amidst the current global economic downturn and will adopt a pragmatic approach to ensure that the requirements are robust and effective against disease transmission, while managing the impact on businesses.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: If we could have a moment of your time.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Therefore, I would invite Leader to come forward to request an extension of the Standing Orders.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This means taking a little more effort to do some simple things, such as binning our litter, returning trays after dining, and practising good toilet etiquette.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It also means having a mindset of consideration for cleaners, and the next person who uses the same public facilities.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Let us build a gracious society, and make Singapore a truly clean and liveable home.      .
